hook: the State of Israel is declared; for Palestinians the same year is the Nakba, the catastrophe; both memories are real

segments.voice: Yesterday, returning to life, and your line: choose life. What was your one life-giving thing? Today a new part of the story opens, after the war, with one year remembered in two ways. Day one thousand twenty-five.

A hall in Tel Aviv, crowded, hot, with a portrait of Theodor Herzl on the wall. David Ben-Gurion stands and reads a declaration aloud. When he finishes, people outside dance in the streets, and some cry, and some just stand there holding the newspaper. In the same season, in towns and villages across the same land, Palestinian families pack what they can carry, or leave with nothing, and lock their doors behind them. Some of them take the keys. In some families, those keys are still kept. Today's word is the year that holds both scenes.
screen: `A DECLARATION READ ALOUD.` → `DANCING IN THE STREETS.` → `A DOOR LOCKED, A KEY KEPT.`

segments.voice: The declaration that founded the State of Israel is dated in its own text, the fourteenth of May, 1948. It calls the land of Israel the birthplace of the Jewish people. It remembers the Holocaust that had just ended. And it makes promises: equal social and political rights for all the state's inhabitants, whatever their religion, race or sex, and a hand held out in peace to its neighbors. For Jews who had survived, after everything these last sessions have carried, it meant a place where the doors would not be closed. In Israel the day is marked as Yom Ha'atzmaut, Independence Day. Some communities add festive psalms of praise to their prayers. Some Haredi communities do not celebrate it as a religious day. And Israelis mark the day before it as a memorial for those who died in its wars. War came quickly. Armies of neighboring Arab states joined the fighting, and the land was torn through. For Palestinians, this is the Nakba, an Arabic word for catastrophe. Families fled or were driven from their homes, villages were emptied, and the families were not allowed back. Palestinians mark it each year, with keys and names of villages. This path is not the place to settle a war or to weigh one sorrow against another. It is a place to say plainly what people remember. For one people, a homecoming. For another, an uprooting. Both are memories held by real families. Both are real.
screen: `A DECLARATION, DATED IN ITS OWN TEXT.` · `EQUAL RIGHTS, AND A HAND IN PEACE.` · `NAKBA: THE CATASTROPHE.` · `TWO MEMORIES OF ONE YEAR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: sit with two memories. Breathe, and let your shoulders drop. Picture two families in the same year. In one home, people are crowded around a radio, laughing and crying at once. In another, a mother turns a key in a lock and walks away with her children. You don't have to choose between them. You don't have to explain either one. Hold them both, one in each hand, for the length of the bell. If you pray, you can pray for both families. If you don't, just let both scenes stay in view, without pushing either one out. The bell holds the time.
1948. The year the State of Israel was declared. For Palestinians, the same year is the Nakba, the catastrophe. Today's word.
Your line: two memories of one year. Today, if this year comes up, listen for the memory you hear less often before you answer. Day one thousand twenty-five.

howItsDone: Israeli Jews mark Yom Ha'atzmaut with celebrations, and some synagogues add festive psalms of praise; it follows Yom HaZikaron, a day of memorial. Palestinians mark the Nakba each year.

Sensitive day. Written to the outline's framing (both memories real), with no ranking and no judgment on the war's causes or conduct. A Keeper, and ideally a reviewer familiar with Palestinian memory of the Nakba, should read the whole teach.
Claims rule: the date is spoken only because the declaration states it in its own text. No refugee counts are given. 'Not allowed back' is stated generally; please check the wording.
'For Jews who had survived... a place where the doors would not be closed' rests on the declaration's own reference to the Holocaust and immigration; please check.
Hook details (Herzl's portrait, the Tel Aviv Museum hall, dancing) are well documented but not in the cited text; please check. 'Some families still keep the keys' is stated generally.
Yom Ha'atzmaut: Hallel recited in some communities; some Haredi communities do not celebrate religiously; Yom HaZikaron precedes it. Please check.
'Armies of neighboring Arab states joined the fighting': kept general and undated.
Editor: 'Jews mark the day as Yom Ha'atzmaut' (read as all Jews, just before saying some Haredi communities do not) became 'In Israel the day is marked as Yom Ha'atzmaut'.
